title: Tokens and Embeddings: How Text Becomes Numbers
oneLiner: Why models read tokens rather than words or characters, how byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary, and how embeddings turn each token into a vector where similar meanings sit close together.
keyTakeaway: A language model never sees text. A tokenizer splits text into tokens (whole common words, pieces of rarer words, punctuation), each mapped to an integer id, and each id is looked up as an embedding vector of hundreds or thousands of numbers. Pricing, context limits and speed are all counted in tokens, and the same content can cost very different amounts depending on language, code style and formatting.
explanation:
A model needs a fixed vocabulary of units to read and predict. Whole words do not work well: there are too many of them, new ones appear constantly (product codes, variable names, typos), and a word the model has never seen would be unreadable. Single characters work for anything but make sequences very long, and long sequences are expensive. Modern tokenizers sit in between: common words get a single token, rarer words are split into reusable pieces, and anything at all can still be spelled out from bytes.

Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is the classic way to build such a vocabulary, and many tokenizers in use today are BPE or close relatives. Start with every character as its own token. Count which adjacent pair appears most often in a large training corpus, merge it into a new token, and repeat tens of thousands of times. Frequent fragments like "ing", "the" and " con" become single tokens early; rare strings stay split. To tokenize new text, the learned merges are applied in the same order. The toy tokenizer below learns merges from a tiny corpus about PLCs and motors, so words from that corpus compress well and unfamiliar ones fall apart into small pieces. Real vocabularies are typically somewhere around 30,000 to a few hundred thousand tokens.

Some consequences worth knowing. In English prose a token averages roughly three quarters of a word (about four characters), but that is only a rule of thumb: code, JSON, long numbers, and many non-English languages take more tokens for the same content. Models struggle with letter-level questions ("how many r characters in this word") partly because they see tokens, not letters. And every API price, rate limit and context window is measured in tokens, input and output usually priced separately, so a bloated prompt pasted into every request is a recurring cost.

Each token id is then turned into an embedding: a vector, a list of numbers, learned during training. Training pushes tokens used in similar contexts towards similar vectors, so direction in this space ends up carrying meaning. Similarity is usually measured with cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between two vectors: 1 means same direction, 0 means unrelated, negative means opposite. Separate embedding models turn a whole sentence or document into one vector, which is what powers semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in a later lesson.

The embedding demo uses hand-placed 2-D vectors so you can see the angles. Real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of dimensions and are not hand-made, and individual dimensions rarely mean anything a person could name; the 2-D picture is only for intuition.
